title: Jury hands down eight recommendations at inquest into death of Londoner Mario Hamel
article: London police took a broadside hit from a coroner's jury Wednesday for letting a "sweet, loving" husband kill himself in a video-monitored and frequently checked police cell.

Police need to do better at monitoring and checking on prisoners in their cells, communicating with people during domestic situations and arrests, and auditing their own work, the five-person jury in the Mario Hamel inquest said.

Lawyers for the coroner's office, the London police department and the police association all suggested in their closing submissions the jury consider only one recommendation: enhancing police station technology so an alert goes off when a cell is missed on routine checks. But the jury came back with eight, wide-ranging recommendations.
That gave small comfort to Hamel's London widow, still angry at police.
"I feel shocked, disappointed, heartbroken. I trusted police. They didn't do their job," Roseena Baksh said.
"I think the jury did see the mistakes that were made and I hope the police take serious action and make sure it doesn't happen again."
When police arrested her husband, they promised to release him once he sobered up, Baksh said.

"It didn't happen that way and I lost him forever, I am not the same person anymore. I have a lot of darkness, a broken heart. I can't move on. I lost the love of my life. He was sweet, loving, caring, affectionate . . ."
The police cadet, now a constable, who forgot to check on her husband in his cell minutes before and after he killed himself showed no remorse at the inquest, Baksh added.
"She didn't get penalized and she became a constable. I am one that lost. My kids lost and my family lost."
Hamel, 55, called 911 himself late at night Nov. 24, 2010.
Drunk and with a thick French-Canadian accent, he tried to explain he'd touched his step-daughter's cheek and didn't want to get into the trouble.
Two constables arrived at the house. They testified at the inquest that Hamel kept trying to touch them, perhaps trying to illustrate something, and grew more agitated.
For his and his family's safety, and with nowhere else to go, Hamel was arrested for being drunk in public and taken to the police station detention unit, the constables testified.
"We assured him it was a matter of him going to sleep for three to four hours," and he'd get out in time for work the next day, Const. Amanda Dymock said.
Baksh gave a different version of events, testifying her husband wasn't agitated - only trying to communicate.
"They didn't listen to him. I said, 'there is no harm in him. Please don't take him.' "
At the station, officers asked Hamel if he was healthy. He said, yes, but was worried about going to jail.

The two arresting officers, the booking sergeant and two cadets on duty all testified Hamel showed no suicidal signs - signs that would have prompted police to put him in a cell close by with a dedicated video monitor.
Instead, Hamel was put in distant cell 18, that shared space on a video monitor with other cells.
At 2:52 a.m., according to videotapes, Hamel sat upright on his cell bench. He took off his shirt, tied one end around his neck and another around the cell door bars.

For the next 11 minutes, Hamel tried three times to hang himself with his shirt before finally succeeding. Through all this, the booking sergeant and two cadets were working at the booking station, where above them the slow suicide played out on a video screen.
At 3:03 a.m., Hamel stopped moving.
Three minutes later, Sinclair did her routine cell checks. She did them again at 3:24 a.m. and 3:47 a.m. But, Sinclair testified, she didn't go to cell 18 to because she forgot Hamel was there.
